t: What to eat in Catania: 10 tastes in order of the day
d: Arancino, granita with brioche, pasta alla Norma, horse meat and Sant'Agata sweets: what to order in Catania, when, and roughly what it costs.
x: Eating in Catania is not solved with a restaurant: it is solved with a well-built day. You start with a granita, pass through the market, have something fried for lunch and finish with a pasta that here has an opera-house name. This guide puts the tastings in the order that makes sense. In short. Morning: granita and brioche. Mid-morning: fish market and street food. Lunch: arancino and pasta alla Norma. Afternoon: sweets. Evening: horse meat or fish, if you like. Prices are indicative averages. Morning Granita with brioche Almond, pistachio, coffee or lemon, with Sicilian brioche. About €4. Mid-morning Fish market and surroundings Watch the market and taste standing up. Lunch Arancino and pasta alla Norma In Catania the fried one is masculine; Norma is the first course not to skip. Afternoon Cannolo and sweets Sheep's ricotta and marzipan. Evening Horse meat or fish One choice, not both. 1. Granita and brioche # The Catanese breakfast is granita (water, sugar and fruit) with a Sicilian brioche, leavened with eggs and scented with vanilla or citrus. The flavours to start from are almond, pistachio, coffee and lemon. If you are short on time, pick just one: coffee granita with cream is the most recognisable. Indicative average cost: about €4. 2. Seltz with lemon and salt # At the city's kiosks they drink a seltz made with lemon juice, sparkling water, salt and a pinch of bicarbonate. It sounds odd until it is hot. About €2. 3. The fish market and its street food # The fish market, which locals call "a piscaria", is a few steps from Piazza Duomo, near the Fountain of the Seven Channels. You do not have to buy anything: just walking through it is a taste of the city. Around it you find kiosks and small places selling food to eat standing up. For hours, practical tips and what to avoid, read the guide to the Catania fish market: hours and how to visit . 4. Arancino (masculine) # In Catania it is arancino, and it has the cone shape that recalls Etna: rice with ragù, breaded and fried. It costs around €2 in bars and simple rosticcerie. If you want a serious comparison, taste the classic ragù one before trying variations. 5. Pasta alla Norma # Pasta with tomato sauce, fried aubergine, salted ricotta and basil. The name recalls Bellini's Norma ; he was born in Catania. It is the first course that best represents the city. In simple trattorie it costs around €8; in smarter places it goes up. 6. Spaghetti alla carrettiera # Oil, raw garlic, pepper and grated pecorin

t: Catania fish market: hours, what to see and how to visit
d: Indicative hours, when to go, what to look at and what to avoid at the Catania fish market, a few steps from Piazza Duomo.
x: The Catania fish market is not an attraction set up for tourists: it is a market that works every morning, loud, wet and beautiful. To visit it well you need a few rules: the right time, the right shoes and an idea of what to look at. In short. Go early in the morning, Monday to Saturday, in closed non-slip shoes. Give the market 30-60 minutes and, if you want to eat, another hour nearby. Sunday is closed. Before 10 Entrance from the Piazza Duomo side The stalls are fully stocked and the light is better. Mid-morning Walk between the stalls Swordfish, tuna, sea bream, sea urchins, octopus. Edges Fruit and vegetables Oranges, broccoli, artichokes: calmer. Afterwards Tastings standing up Street food nearby. Hours: what we know and what we do not # The sources we consulted agree on two points: the market is open Monday to Saturday and closed on Sunday. On exact hours they differ slightly: one says about 7 am to 2 pm, another 8 am to 2:30 pm. That is why the practical rule is the safest one: arrive by mid-morning. After noon some stalls are already packing up, and the best produce is gone. When to go # The best window is before 10: full choice and less heat, especially in summer. The busiest time is around 8:30-10:30. If you want to take photos, choose a weekday and make eye contact with the vendors before shooting. Where it is # In the historic centre, a few metres from Piazza Duomo and near the Fountain of the Seven Channels. From the north you can enter through Porta Uzeda, from the south through Piazza Duomo. From the central station it takes about 10 minutes on foot. What to see # They sell swordfish, tuna, sea bream, sea bass, red mullet, sea urchins and octopus, and by weight clams, cuttlefish and mussels. At the edges there are fruit and vegetable stalls, including Sicilian IGP blood oranges, broccoli and artichokes: they are calmer and let you breathe between one stall and the next. What to bring and what to avoid # Closed shoes with a non-slip sole. The floor is wet and slippery. Strollers and wheelchairs: hard at peak hours, and there are no ramps inside. Fish to cook later: risky in the heat if you cannot keep it cold. Photos of vendors without asking: a nod is enough. Where to eat nearby # Around the market there are kiosks, bars and small trattorie, and by mid-morning street-food stands appear selling things like stigghiola and pane con la milza. t: What to do in Catania when it rains: 7 indoor ideas
d: Rain in Catania? Seven places under a roof, a sensible order to see them and how to rewrite your day without wasting the afternoon.
x: In Catania rain does not ruin the day: it moves it. The historic centre is compact, distances between stops are short and many of the most interesting places are indoors. You only need a sensible order, so you do not cross half the city in the downpour. In short. Keep the stops close, alternate an indoor place with a short outdoor stretch, and check opening hours: museums and monuments change days and time slots. First rule: stay in one area # The worst route in the rain is the one that jumps from one end of the city to the other. Pick one area and fill it: the stretch between Via Etnea, Piazza Duomo and the fish market is the most comfortable, because everything is a few minutes on foot. Provalo ☔ Piove ☀ Non piove 1. Teatro Massimo Bellini Al coperto # The theatre named after Vincenzo Bellini is one of the city's landmark places, right in the centre. If there is no performance on, check whether guided visits are offered: availability changes during the year. 2. Castello Ursino and the civic museum Al coperto # The Swabian-era castle houses the civic museum. It is a solid stop for an hour or two indoors and takes a few minutes to reach from the Duomo area. 3. Monastery of the Benedictines of San Nicolò l'Arena Al coperto # One of the great monastic complexes in Europe, now a university campus and part of the UNESCO listing of the late Baroque towns of the Val di Noto. Guided visits usually need a booking: if it rains, decide early in the morning. 4. The Cathedral of Sant'Agata Al coperto # The Duomo faces Piazza Duomo, with the Elephant Fountain and the Liotru, the symbol of the city. The interior is a perfect shelter for a break between two outdoor stretches. 5. The Achillean Baths under the Cathedral Al coperto # In the basements of the Duomo area there are Roman-era rooms. It is the classic stop you do not know you want until it rains: dry, unusual and very close to the centre. 6. Lunch at the fish market, but under cover All'aperto # The fish market is the popular heart of Catania, mostly outdoors and in the morning. When it rains, the answer is to arrive early and sit down in one of the covered places nearby, instead of walking between the stalls. 7. A proper coffee break Al coperto # In Catania an hour's pause between two stops is not wasted time: it is the best way to let the storm pass. t: Rome in two days: an itinerary that does not wear you out
d: Two days in Rome in a sensible order: stops grouped by area, hours to check and how not to spend the day in a queue.
x: You can see Rome in two days if you accept one rule: do not try to see everything. The city is made of layers, and the more you try to cover it, the more time you spend between stops. The secret is to group it by area. In short. Day one: ancient Rome. Day two: historic centre and Vatican, in an order that depends on bookings. Always check opening hours and access rules. Day 1 · morning Colosseum, Forum and Palatine A single route: book ahead to avoid the queue. Day 1 · lunch Monti A more genuine neighbourhood a few minutes from the Colosseum. Day 1 · afternoon Capitoline Hill and the centre The view over the Forum, then on foot into the historic centre. Day 2 · morning Vatican Museums and St Peter's To be booked, and the longest part of the day. Day 2 · afternoon Pantheon, Navona, Trevi All close, a few minutes' walk apart. Day 2 · evening Trastevere A stroll with no plan. Consiglio Put the booked stops on the same day and keep the other one free: if it rains or you are tired, you move the free part, not the one with a ticket. Quale giorno ti serve? Entrambi Giorno 1 Giorno 2 Day 1: ancient Rome # Morning: Colosseum, Forum and Palatine. They are close and are often visited on a single route: check the official site for how tickets and hours work. Booking ahead avoids the worst of the queue. Lunch around Monti. A few minutes' walk from the Colosseum, it is a neighbourhood with less touristy places than the area immediately around the monuments. Afternoon: Capitoline Hill and the centre. Climb the Capitoline Hill for the view over the Forum and continue on foot towards the historic centre. Day 2: historic centre and Vatican # One decision matters here: the Vatican takes time and usually a booking. If you want to see it, put it in the morning and keep the rest of the day lighter. Morning: Vatican Museums and St Peter's. Check closing days and entry rules on the official site. Afternoon: Pantheon, Piazza Navona and Trevi. They are all close, a few minutes' walk from one another. For the Pantheon, check the entry rules. Evening: Trastevere. A stroll with no plan is the right way to finish. The three rules that make the difference # Group by area. No zig-zagging. Book the most requested places, leave the rest free. Leave one empty hour each day. Rome gets better when you are not in a hurry. t: One day in Ortigia: a walking itinerary, without rushing
d: How to see Ortigia in a day: order of the stops, where to slow down and what to leave out so it does not turn into a marathon.
x: Ortigia is small, and that is exactly why it is easy to get wrong: you cross it in a rush trying to see everything and leave feeling you have not really looked at it. This itinerary does the opposite. Few stops, an order that makes sense and room to pause. In short. Market in the morning, Duomo and square around midday, seafront and the Fountain of Arethusa in the late afternoon. The rest you choose by mood. Morning Ortigia market The starting point: arrive early, taste standing up and leave before the crowd. Late morning Duomo and square The Greek temple inside the Baroque cathedral, and five minutes on the square. Lunch Side streets Two blocks from the square are enough to change quality and prices. Early afternoon Inner streets and the Giudecca Without a plan, keeping an eye out for guided visits. Late afternoon Fountain of Arethusa and seafront As far as Castello Maniace, in the low light. A che ora sei a Ortigia? 09:00 Morning: the market # Ortigia's market is a good starting point: it runs in the morning and it is where you immediately grasp the island's atmosphere. Arrive early, taste something standing up and leave the stalls before they get crowded. Late morning: Duomo and square # Syracuse Cathedral is built around the remains of a Greek temple dedicated to Athena: the Doric columns are still visible in the side walls. It is a rare example of centuries layered in the same building. The square in front, with its façade, is worth five minutes before moving on. Lunch without hurry # Ortigia lends itself to long lunches. Avoid trattorie with a tourist menu at the door and look for the side streets: two blocks from the square are enough to change quality and prices. Early afternoon: the inner streets # Let yourself get lost in the maze of lanes. In the Giudecca area you find traces of the Jewish presence in Syracuse. If guided visits interest you, check days and times in advance. Late afternoon: Fountain of Arethusa and seafront # The Fountain of Arethusa is a freshwater spring a few steps from the sea, tied to an ancient myth. From here the walk along the sea leads to Castello Maniace, at the tip of the island. The best moment is when the light drops. What to leave out # Too many museums in the same day: one, well chosen, is enough. Out-and-back trips: follow a loop. The idea of "having seen everything": Ortigia gets better with every return. t: AI travel itineraries: what works and what does not
d: How to use AI to plan a trip without letting it invent places that do not exist: what to ask, what to check and why real places matter.
x: Asking an AI "plan me three days in Palermo" always works, in the sense that an answer arrives. The point is another: is it right? A good itinerary is not a well-written list, it is a sequence of real places, open, reachable in the order it proposes. And that is where things get complicated. In short. AI is excellent at putting things in order and giving ideas, mediocre when it has to guarantee that a place exists and is open. The difference is made by the real data under the answer. What AI does well # It orders. It turns ten scattered ideas into a day with a logical thread. It adapts. If you say "I am with kids" or "I only have half a day", the angle changes. It explains. It tells you why a place is worth it, not just where it is. What it does badly # It invents with confidence. A generic model can suggest a restaurant that has closed, a museum that does not exist, a wrong opening time. It ignores geography. It can line up stops that are half an hour apart on foot on the map. It does not know it is raining today. Unless it receives the data, it does not adapt the programme to the day. How to use it without getting hurt # Give precise context: area, days, pace, who you travel with. Ask for close stops, grouped by neighbourhood. Check every stop on a map: does it exist, where is it, how far from the previous one. Check opening hours on the official source. Ask for a plan B for rain or tiredness. Why real places make the difference # A system designed for travel starts from the opposite end: real places first, with their coordinates, then the AI that orders and narrates them. That way it cannot suggest a place that is not there, because it does not fish it out of its memory. It is the idea behind UNNIVAI: a route made of real places, built around your time and your tastes, and rewritten when the day changes. Concrete examples # The rule holds for every city: try it on the guides Rome in two days and Ortigia in one day , where every stop has a place, an area and a time. The five-minute test # Before trusting any itinerary, even your own: pick three stops at random and check them on the map. If all three exist, are close and are open, the rest usually holds. If even one fails, start again. Fai il test adesso Prendi tre tappe del tuo itinerario e spunta ciò che hai verificato.
